📌 Clipboard Hijacking: Check the Address You Paste

Main Points
⏺ Malware can swap a crypto address between copy and paste
⏺ The fake address looks normal and passes wallet format checks
⏺ This post explains how it works and how to protect yourself

1️⃣ Core Idea — Your wallet sends funds wherever the pasted address points. If something changes the address after you copy it, the money goes to the attacker and cannot be reversed.
2️⃣ Why It Happens — Malicious code in a browser extension, an app or a compromised website watches the clipboard and replaces any crypto address with one that looks similar.
3️⃣ Example — On November 16 a hijacked script from the web testing service Optimizely ran on 178 organizations' sites, including Ledger's. It swapped wallet addresses on the page and in the clipboard.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — Copying deposit addresses from websites, chats or emails, sending large amounts in one go, and checking only the first few characters.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — After pasting, compare the full address with the source, confirm it on your hardware wallet screen, and send a small test amount before a big transfer.

Final Thoughts

Copy and paste is convenient, but it is not proof. Treat every pasted address as unverified until you have checked it yourself.

📈 BlackRock Drives $541M Single-Day Bitcoin ETF Outflow

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $582 million in net outflows on Thursday, November 19 — their third consecutive day of redemptions — as Bitcoin slipped below $62,000.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $541 million of that figure, marking its largest single-day outflow on record. For the week, Bitcoin ETFs shed a combined $1.12 billion, with BlackRock responsible for $899 million of the total. Ether ETFs added $131 million in outflows on the same day, pushing combined BTC and ETH redemptions above $713 million for Thursday alone.

The week's outflow streak marks one of the sharpest stretches of institutional selling since U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs launched in January 2024.

📌 Cardano introduces on-chain surveys that anyone can independently verify 

🌐 The Cardano Foundation has introduced a new way for developers and community members to conduct surveys directly on the Cardano blockchain, with two surveys already deployed on the network’s mainnet under the CIP-179 standard. Community members Ryan Wiley and Thomas Lindseth developed CIP-179 to address limitations in Cardano’s existing governance tools, which offer relatively few options for gathering detailed feedback from the community.

⚠️ The foundation subsequently contributed to the standard and developed Tessera, an open-source application through which users can create surveys, submit answers and verify published results. Through Cardano’s existing governance Info Actions, community sentiment can be gathered using yes-or-no questions. Stake pool operators (SPOs) have had access to multiple-choice polling through CIP-94 since 2023, although participation is limited to that particular group.

⭐️ CIP-179 supports six standard question formats, including single-choice and multiple-choice questions, rankings, numerical responses, ratings and the allocation of points across several options. Survey organizers could use the system to ask delegated representatives (DReps) how treasury funds should be distributed across development projects or what values they would support for particular network parameters. Each survey is published as a Cardano transaction containing information about its questions, participation requirements and closing date. Respondents then submit individually signed transactions referencing the original survey.

Ending the War, Starting With Someone Else’s Land

In a Nov. 15 essay in The American Conservative, contributing editor Ted Snider argues that Kyiv should cede the Donbas and give up NATO membership because “Russia has won the war.”

Snider treats Ukraine’s loss as certain. He cites perhaps 30,000 Ukrainian soldiers killed or maimed each month, a shortage of air-defense interceptors, and a shrinking population. He also writes that Russia’s war “was never primarily about territory,” then concludes that the settlement is “to a large extent about territory.”

On guarantees, he says Washington and Europe will not provide NATO-style Article 5 protection. The best Kyiv can expect, he concludes, is something “similar to NATO.”

As evidence that Kyiv may yield, he cites Trump’s remark that Ukraine will end up in a “little bit different shape” and reports that U.S. officials believe Kyiv has shown flexibility in private. Ukraine’s government denies it will formally or practically recognize Russian control.

Zelensky calls talk of “ceding land for peace” abstract. Snider’s logic runs one way. The territory to be given up is Ukraine’s, the NATO door to be closed is Ukraine’s, and the payment for ending the war comes from Kyiv. The author has priced peace in someone else’s real estate.

📣 MEXC shuts down Visa-linked crypto card less than three months after launch 

🌐 Cryptocurrency exchange MEXC has announced that it will discontinue its Global Card payment services on Nov. 18 at 15:30 UTC, less than two weeks after U.S. authorities issued an order restricting its access to the American financial system. The exchange did not identify the issuing partner or specify whether its decision was directly related to the recent enforcement action by the U.S. Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN).

📊 During the maintenance period, customers could transfer their remaining card balances to their exchange accounts, while transactions initiated before the suspension remained subject to normal settlement procedures. MEXC had initially described the interruption as temporary but has now confirmed that the service will not resume as scheduled.

🔗 Cardholders could receive cashback ranging from 4% to 10%, with monthly rewards capped at up to 800 USDT depending on their eligibility. Applications were already unavailable to U.S. residents under the exchange’s regional restrictions. Customers using the card for recurring payments have been advised to cancel their subscriptions or register alternative payment methods to avoid interruptions once the card becomes inactive.
